487	Blessed be He, the love of a Father behind the pain. Every
488	child who gets punished by his father knows that at first, of course,
489	the feeling is one of anger and resentment. Why did Dad abandon
490	me? Why is Dad treating me this way? But it takes
491	wisdom to understand what Dad means. It takes
492	greatness of soul to rise above the spontaneous pain
493	and hear Dad's inner rebuke: I will not
494	let you fall. My expectations of you are too great
495	for me to let you do foolish things. This is the strength of
496	Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Akiva, who looks into the depths of
497	things. A man who is all good, a man who is all faith,
498	a man whose head is in the heavens. So on this hard night
499	they come to Rabbi Akiva to be comforted. The teachers come
500	to the student to receive from him the strength to go on,
501	onward,
502	and to hold on even in the hard moments of exile, with confidence
503	and with the knowledge that great things are happening, and that these days
504	will yet create strength, create connection, create a bond
505	that all the hard days could not create.
506	Let us mention in this context an idea that is simple,
507	wonderful, sublime, an idea that fills the heart with strength,
508	that truly gives something to hold on to in these last moments
509	of the exile.
510	The custom of the Sephardim, the custom of the Eastern communities,
511	is to begin the Kinot on the night of Tisha beAv with the kinah of
512	Haazinu.
513	Even before the other Kinot, they begin
514	to read the kinah of Haazinu, the terrible prophecies of destruction
515	that Moshe Rabbeinu said. The kinah of Haazinu foretells
516	bad days, hard days that the greatest prophets of the destruction
517	did not expect the like of. Moshe Rabbeinu says verses
518	that are hard even to repeat. He quotes
519	the Holy One, Blessed be He: "I said," days will come when the Holy One,
520	Blessed be He, will say, "I would scatter them to the corners,"
521	I will cast them out like the corner of the field. I will throw the people of
522	Israel to the corners of the world, one Jew here, one Jew
523	there, so that they lose completely their meaning. Grain
524	that is concentrated, that is gathered, has importance, has
525	weight, has volume, has meaning. But
526	when you throw one stalk here and one stalk
527	there, and one kernel here and one kernel there, it has
528	no validity, no meaning, no
529	weight. "I would scatter them to the corners": I will cast the people of Israel
530	to the corner of the world like merchandise that no one wants, like
531	merchandise no one desires. And He goes on and says terrible words:
532	"I would make their memory cease from among men."
533	Days will come when the Holy One, Blessed be He, will want to wipe out
534	the people of Israel, not only the body, Heaven forbid, but
535	the memory of the people of Israel, so that no one will remember that there once was
536	a people of Israel. The destruction will be so total, acute,
537	and terrible that no one will remember that there once was such a phenomenon
538	called the chosen people of the Holy One, Blessed be He.
539	And why will He not do it? Why are we here,
540	thank God, alive and kicking? "Were it not that I feared the anger of the
541	enemy, lest their adversaries misjudge." Only so that the enemy
542	will not win.
543	I will not wipe out the people of Israel, only so as not to let
544	Hitler win. We can imagine to what lowliness the people of
545	Israel would come, that the people of Israel remain alive in the world: a Father
546	leaves his son alive in the world not because the son deserves
547	mercy, only so that the enemy will not claim victory.
548	We can imagine terrible and dreadful things. There are no more
549	harsh and terrible prophecies than the kinah of
550	Haazinu. And here one question arises: so why is it a song?
551	Why is Haazinu a song and not a lament on the night of Tisha beAv,
552	when the Eastern communities read it as a kinah?
553	But all year it is a song. First, in the Torah itself it
554	is written in rhyme. Second, it is written like two
555	columns with a break in the middle, the way a song is written. Third,
556	in the Beit HaMikdash the Levites would sing it, literally
557	with song and melody. Every Shabbat they would sing "Hazeiv lecha."
558	"Hazeiv lecha" means they would divide the song of Haazinu
559	into six parts, and every Shabbat they would sing one part.
560	Accordingly, in the synagogue we divide
561	the first part of Haazinu into six aliyot. "Hazeiv lecha":
562	"Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak; remember the days of old," "He rode on
563	the high places of the earth." We divide the song of Haazinu into six
564	parts
565	and read the first six aliyot the way
566	the Levites would sing in the Beit HaMikdash. They sing six Shabbatot
567	and then start over again. How can we
568	understand what the Levites sang? "I said, I would scatter them"
569	to the corners: in what melody did they sing it? This is
570	after all about terrible prophecies of exile, which one should read
571	sitting on the ground on the night of Tisha beAv,
572	and the Levites would sing suffering, sing pain. An enormous question:
573	what lies here? Is Haazinu a song, or is Haazinu
574	a kinah? How can we understand the whole matter?
575	The Rebbe once said a truly brilliant thing in Likutei Sichot,
576	in a short note he said it, but it is truly something
577	so special.
578	Haazinu is a song because it films the entire path.
579	Haazinu is a song because it is a panoramic picture
580	of all the chapters, all the sections in the life of the people of
581	Israel. Haazinu, says the Ramban, portrays past, present,
582	and future. In the song of Haazinu, the suffering, the pain, the
583	terrible kinah is a chapter
584	within the great plan that leads to the redemption.
585	And over this a Jew sings: not over this moment, but over the understanding
586	that this moment produces redemption, produces good,
587	produces a greatness that the good days did not produce.
588	A Jew does not sing over this moment as it is, but over
589	this moment as it is part of the movement of the train, part
590	of the progress of the ship,
591	of the progress of the route, part of the trouble
592	that becomes a skylight and builds the future redemption. Let us
593	see: here He began with the past, "He found him in a desert land,"
594	"He encircled him, He bore him," "as an eagle stirs up its nest, hovers over its young."
595	The days after the Exodus from Egypt, the giving of the Torah:
596	the Holy One, Blessed be He, carried us like an eagle on the wings
597	of eagles. We were at the top of the world, at the peak of the world.
598	And then comes the destruction, the terrible exile.
